comments.author: @TheEarthEngineOfficial
comments.text: The Narva/Ivangorod example is the part that makes the thought experiment land — the same river, two towns, and the border alone seems to decide which side prospers. It raises a sharper question than land versus people, though: how much of the gap is the institutions that moved with the people, rather than the rivers themselves?

replies.author: @TheEarthEngineOfficial
replies.text: That's an honest answer — and honestly, the question is hard even for economists, because swapping the maps wouldn't swap the tax systems, the prices, or the institutions. If you had to pick just one thing that makes the biggest difference between the two economies, what would you guess it is?

replies.author: @T_T408
replies.text: ​@TheEarthEngineOfficial думаю я слишком молод и несвудущь в экономике для однозначного ответа😅

replies.author: @TheEarthEngineOfficial
replies.text: That's a fair point — the tax systems and the price levels really are two different worlds, and swapping the maps wouldn't swap either of them. It makes me wonder how much of the gap is the tax structure itself, and how much is what sits underneath it: the resources, the distances, the way each economy is built. Which of those do you think moves the numbers most?
